transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Hugo (Redwood SE), Ellen, Tom, Priya, Jordan (Solaris)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/rec/ff-20261029-6482 (internal)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC review focused on scorecard regressions from last run, prompt-set pruning experiments, and a short fallback/canary readiness drill. Customer is seeing a small uptick in false positives on classification of inbound exceptions; want to validate rollback thresholds and dedicated capacity economics.

Topics covered:
- Recent eval run (10/27) results and heatmap
- Guardrail false-positive spike and prompt surgery ideas
- Scoring thresholds and how to tune for high precision vs recall
- Canary/fallback plan and VPC/on-prem constraints
- Next steps: pricing, security docs, and a scheduled canary run

Action items on call (discussed verbally, items below captured in notes):
- Ravi will output threshold CSV + short doc explaining rationale
- Maya to share Dedicated pricing + pilot SOW draft
- Solaris to provision VPC peering for canary run

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): All right, thanks everyone for joining, we'll run through the recent quality run and then do a quick readiness checklist for the fallback. Ellen, do you want to kick off with what you saw on the heatmap?
[00:12] Ellen (Solaris): Yeah sure, thanks. So the 10-27 eval, we used the new prompt-slice set B that Priya put together, and overall accuracy is similar but the false positive rate on 'shipment exception' calls jumped about 5 points, which is... it's not crippling but it is material for our ops team.
[00:30] Priya (Solaris): yep, and just to add, some of the prompts in set B were longer with more context, that might be affecting the KV caching — or, I dunno, the KV cash as the transcript will probably say — but we did see more hallucinated exception labels on edge cases.
[00:48] Ravi (Redwood SE): Okay, got it. Are those edge cases skewed toward short messages or ones with obfuscated SKUs? Any common signal?
[00:56] Priya: Mostly short messages with abbreviated locations, like "stk rcvd" or codes. The model tends to over-classify when the prompt contains ambiguous tokens.
[01:10] Hugo (Redwood): Quick question — which model/bundle did you run on? Was that the hosted m-8k-quant or the dedicated rwd-small we set up?
[01:18] Ellen: That was on the hosted m-8k-quant variant, we haven't switched to the dedicated pool yet. We did one smoke on the dedicated yesterday but didn't use it for the eval.
[01:26] Maya: Ok that matters because quantization profile and tokenization mismatch can cause subtle shifts. Ravi, can you pull up the score distribution and the per-slice precision/recall?
[01:36] Ravi: Yeah grabbing it now, I'm looking at the heatmap share Hugo uploaded — link in chat — but high level the precision for the exception class dropped from 0.88 to 0.83 and recall is steady at 0.73. The bin around low-confidence scores 0.4-0.6 expanded.
[01:58] Tom (Solaris): That 0.4-0.6 bin is where our human-in-the-loop kicks in, but operations can't handle tripling in that band. We need better gating or stronger guardrails.
[02:10] Maya: Right, so two levers — tighten scoring threshold (raise decision threshold) or tune prompts to reduce ambiguity. Tightening reduces recall but improves precision.
[02:22] Ellen: Can you show what a tightened threshold would look like in throughput loss?
[02:28] Ravi: If we move the cut from 0.5 to 0.62, we'd drop false positives by ~40% on this slice, but we'd also drop throughput of auto-handled events by about 18% — more human reviews.
[02:42] Jordan (Solaris): Ops budget won't love that. Is there a middle ground like tiered routing? E.g., auto for >0.75, canary for 0.6-0.75, human for <0.6.
[02:52] Hugo: Yes, Redwood runtime supports tiered routing. You can route by score to a canary model variant or to the dedicated pool with different latency SLOs.
[03:02] Priya: If we route 0.6-0.75 to a canary smaller model, do we get better precision?
[03:07] Ravi: Sometimes. The smaller model (rwd-small) is less likely to hallucinate on short prompts, but it depends on how much context you strip. We can also try prefix caching to stabilize the KV cache across calls.
[03:20] Ellen: Prefix caching — are we talking about persistent KV cache across sessions?
[03:23] Ravi: Yeah, so if you have repeated phrases or SKU prefixes, keeping them hot in the KV cache reduces variability. But it's sensitive to user-level keys and privacy considerations.
[03:33] Tom: On privacy, we need to see how that interacts with our PII removal pipeline. We can't keep raw SKUs in cache unless they're hashed.
[03:40] Maya: Good flag. We'll add a note for the engineer team: PV-PII and cache hashing.
[03:45] Ellen: Also quick question about rollback — if we do a canary and it regresses, what's the fastest rollback?
[03:51] Hugo: Canary rollbacks are instant server-side. We keep a stable model variant and rollout policy; if metrics cross failure thresholds you can auto-fallback to stable or to a cheaper hosted variant.
[04:02] Maya: We documented a rollback RPC in the SOW, but we'll demo it during the drill.
[04:07] Jordan: I want to see a live drill where you force a regression and we watch the automatic fallback. Can that be scheduled next week?
[04:12] Maya: Yes, Tuesday 11/03 works on our side. Does that fit Solaris?
[04:17] Tom: Tue works. We'll provision VPC peering over the weekend and give you a test token.
[04:22] Priya: On the scoring thresholds — are you going to provide a CSV of new cutpoints per class?
[04:27] Ravi: Yes. I'll produce a per-class CSV, plus a short rationale doc that shows expected precision/recall tradeoffs and throughput delta. I'll link the sample heatmap too.
[04:33] Ellen: Please include the guardrail gating rules in plain English — our compliance folks need it for approvals.
[04:39] Maya: We'll attach the SOC 2 summary and KMS architecture note. Are you using Google KMS or AWS KMS?
[04:44] Tom: AWS KMS for keys, but we also want an HSM option for the Private deployment later.
[04:50] Hugo: HSM integration is supported in Private deployments; we can outline the steps. For this pilot the hosted key wrapping with AWS KMS is fine.
[04:57] Priya: Another small thing — tokenization mismatch earlier, we had a slightly different tokenizer when quantizing. Could that produce some of the shift?
[05:04] Ravi: Absolutely. If token boundaries change you can see score drift. We recommend a pinned tokenizer + quantization profile for the evaluation window.
[05:12] Maya: We'll put that in the SOW notes: pinned tokenizer and quant profile for the next eval.
[05:18] Ellen: ok. Also, one weird failure mode — some of the examples that fail are multi-lingual bits like Spanish city names. Are we doing any locale normalization?
[05:28] Priya: We do minimal normalization now but can add a preprocessor step for common locales.
[05:33] Ravi: That would help. Also, for the canary run we can enable per-slice logging and attach additional metadata so you can triage quickly.
[05:42] Jordan: Can that metadata be turned off automatically after the drill for PII reasons?
[05:46] Hugo: Yes, logging levels and retention are configurable per-route. We can set a short TTL for any sensitive logs.
[05:52] Tom: On pricing — can you send a dedicated capacity estimate for the pilot duration (4 weeks) and also show burst vs reserved delta?
[05:59] Maya: Sure, I'll send a draft. We can provide monthly reserved pricing and an elastic burst add-on.
[06:05] Ellen: One more question — we saw a small increase in latency during the last hosted run, possibly because of batching. Any suggestions to keep P95 under 120ms?
[06:14] Ravi: Continuous batching can raise tail latency if knobbed for throughput. For low latency SLO you want smaller batch windows, and possibly dedicated pool with pinned GPUs. Also kernel selection matters; we can force low-latency kernels for the critical route.
[06:27] Priya: Is that more expensive?
[06:29] Hugo: Typically yes. Low-latency profile increases unit cost per token because batching efficiencies drop. We'll show the delta in the cost estimate.
[06:35] Ellen: ok. For the canary drill, can we run a synthetic load that mirrors our production traffic so the rollback is realistic?
[06:42] Ravi: Yep, send the sample workload trace and we'll replay it against the canary variant.
[06:48] Jordan: We'll anonymize the trace and share by Monday.
[06:51] Maya: Great. Quick recap: Ravi will send thresholds CSV and heatmap artifact, Maya will share pricing + SOC2 + KMS note, Solaris to provision VPC peering and share token, schedule canary drill for Tue 11/03.
[07:04] Ellen: Sounds good. Anything else?
[07:07] Tom: Just a procedural ask — can you include a short step-by-step rollback runbook that our oncall can follow?
[07:14] Hugo: Yep, we'll include a one-page rollback runbook and the RPC calls you can use.
[07:19] Priya: Also, if you could include an example prompt surgery (before/after) that would help our prompt authors.
[07:26] Ravi: I'll attach 3 example prompt edits and their measured impact.
[07:30] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up in chat and cut the tasks. Thanks everyone.

[07:36] (call ends)
